s0.open.text: These are two companies in the same industry. [[0.35]] When the market has a good year, they both have a good year. When it falls, they both fall.

s0.weather.text: So if one of them goes up, you have learned almost nothing. You are looking at the weather.

s0.gap.text: Look at the distance between them instead. [[0.4]] Most of the year it holds. And then, here, it stretches.

s0.question.text: Which is the whole question. [[0.5]] When is a gap big enough to bet on?

s1.beta.text: First, make the gap a real number. [[0.35]] Stretch B until it sits on top of A. That is all beta does: it says how many shares of B match one share of A.

s1.lift.text: What is left over, the part that does not line up, is the gap. [[0.3]] On its own, that is one number a day, for a year.

s1.obvious.text: Now the obvious rule. Pick a number of dollars, and call anything past it unusual. [[0.4]] Two dollars.

s1.silent.text: And for a hundred and ten days, it never fires. Not once. The gap never gets that far from home.

s1.shout.text: And now, over the next hundred and thirty days, it fires on ninety-eight of them. [[0.45]] Something that is true almost every day is not telling you anything.

s1.lesson.text: There is no dollar number that works, because the pair is quiet in one stretch and loud in the other. [[0.4]] Two dollars is a fact about dollars, not about this pair.

s2.need.text: What the threshold is missing is a unit. [[0.4]] And there is only one honest place to get one: the gap's own recent past.

s2.window.text: Take the last sixty days. Their average is where the gap has been sitting. [[0.3]] How far they scatter around it is how far it usually wanders.

s2.band.text: Slide that window along, and you get a band. [[0.4]] Watch it breathe. Narrow where the pair is quiet, wide where it is loud.

s2.ruler.text: So ask the same question in units of the band. [[0.45]] Not how many dollars. How many band-widths.

s2.rescale.text: Nothing about the gap has changed. We are only measuring it differently. [[0.35]] Straighten the band into rails, and the curve comes with it, now in units of its own noise.

s2.z.text: That number has a name. The gap, minus its rolling mean, divided by its rolling standard deviation. [[0.4]] The z-score.

s3.rule.text: And now the rule is testable. [[0.35]] Outside the rails, bet that the gap closes: sell the expensive one, buy the cheap one. Back at the middle, close.

s3.market.text: Notice what you are not doing. You are not predicting the market: both legs ride it together, so it cancels.

s3.six.text: Six times on this stretch of data, it did. [[0.4]] Six trades, six winners, three dollars seventy-five.

s3.but.text: But look closely at the first two.

s3.cost.text: The gap came back twenty-seven cents, and then twenty-four. [[0.35]] Getting in and out of both legs costs about twenty. So those trades kept seven cents, and four.

s3.strip.text: Here is that cost, on the same picture. [[0.3]] A fixed number of dollars. But sigma is not fixed, so in band-widths the cost breathes the other way.

s3.same.text: Which is why the same signal made four cents in the quiet stretch, and a dollar fifty-eight in the loud one. [[0.4]] Two sigma is worth thirty cents when sigma is fifteen.

s4.fitted.text: Now the uncomfortable part. [[0.4]] Sixty days. Two sigma. Every one of those numbers was chosen by looking at this picture.

s4.holdout.text: So the only test worth anything is the part of the picture we have not looked at. [[0.45]] Here it is.

s4.enter.text: The gap goes low. The rule buys. [[0.3]] And then the gap keeps going.

s4.walk.text: Nine dollars. [[0.3]] Eleven. [[0.4]] And it does not come back. The relationship did not stretch. It ended.

s4.z.text: And watch the z-score while that happens. [[0.4]] Over the whole collapse it never once passes minus two and a half. On the day the gap is eleven dollars from home, the z-score reads minus one point four.

s4.why.text: It is not lying. It is answering the question you asked: is today unusual, compared with the last sixty days. [[0.45]] And the last sixty days are falling too. The mean is chasing the gap down.

s4.tally.text: Six winners. Three dollars seventy-five. [[0.5]] One trade back: nine dollars and thirty-two cents, and eighty-nine days spent holding it, waiting for a mean that had already left.

s5.restate.text: So. [[0.5]] When is a gap big enough to bet on?

s5.answer.text: Never in dollars. [[0.45]] Only in sigmas. And only while the sigmas are still measuring something that is there.

s5.ruler.text: Because what we built was never a prediction. [[0.35]] It was a ruler, made out of the recent past, and then handed the assumption that the recent past still applies.

s5.close.text: Which is why the real work is not finding the signal. [[0.4]] It is out-of-sample testing, and costs, and position sizing, and drawdowns. Machinery for one question: how much of the edge was ever there.
